Background 
We are Cub Scout Pack 323 from Moscow, Idaho, and our pack currently consists of 12 kids ranging from 5 to 
11 years of age. Our pack loves to learn about science, which is a part of every Cub Scout rank and help prepare 
these amazing kids for life, and who knows maybe one of them will be a future scientist on the Moon. We learned 
a lot from participating in the Plan Mars Challenge in the summer of 2021 which we have used to make some 
improvement for this challenge. We would like to say a big thank you to Idaho Space Grant for giving us the 
opportunity to participate in this challenge. THANK YOU! 
Experiment design 
Cub Scout Pack 323 – Team Wheat chose to plant 5 spring wheat seeds and 5 spring pea seeds in five of the pots 
in different ratio of Lunar regolith and Blue Ribbon Organics OMRI Certified Natural Premium Organic Compost 
for Plants. In the other five pots we planted only spring wheat so we can test if there is a symbiotic relationship 
between wheat grown with peas versus wheat grown by themselves. We used the compost because it provides an 
organic media for the plants to grow in, and it help provide nutrients and retain water. It also provides microbes 
that could be beneficial for plant growth. It would also be a compost which could be similar to what astronauts 
would be able to produce on site on the moon. We added the recommended dose of all-purpose Miracle-Gro 
fertilizer weekly to the wheat/peas pots and the wheat only pots. The fertilizer is a standard way to stimulate plant 
growth and would need to be transported from Earth. We decided to set up our experiments in a lab at the 
University of Idaho where we could provide our plants a more stable environment without temperature 
fluctuations as we had issues with last time. LED growth lights was used during the entire growth period to help 
our plants grow, this was small LED lights that was evenly spread out above the plants and gave all our plants the 
same amount of light. Growth was measured as the height of the plants, we measured the tallest and the shorts 
plants every time, and the highest measurement is the one that will be used when assessing our results.

Independent variables & dependent variables 
The independent variables in Cub Scout Pack 323’s wheat experiment is the amount of light, 1 dose of fertilizer 
and 50 ml of water given to our plants per day, except through Spring break where all plants suffered equally a 
bit from lack of watering as seen in the pictures with especially the peas drying out. The first dependent variables 
in our experiment are the spring wheat and spring pea combo versus the spring wheat by themselves, and the 
second dependent variable is the different ratio of Lunar regolith and compost from 50/50 to 75/25. 
Measurements 
As a measurement of our plant’s success, we chose to measure the height of the plants and we reuse the point 
system that we used last time as a measurement for how well the plants were thriving (0=no plant, 1=shrivel/died, 
2=okay, 3=good). We decided to add 50ml of water to each pot every day to simplify the process for the kids.

Like wheat, pea height tended to increase until approximately 
day 20 after which plant height tended plateaued. Increasing 
lunar regolith content tended to have less of an influence on pea 
height. 
The total plant biomass was greatest in the controls, with the wheat only control 
having the greatest biomass overall. For the wheat and pea treatment, biomass 
was greatest in the 70% lunar regolith treatment, with increasing biomass 
observed from 50% to 70% followed by a decline in biomass at 75% lunar 
regolith. A similar pattern was observed in the wheat only treatment, but 
biomass peaked at 60% lunar regolith. The lowest biomass was observed in the 
wheat only treatment grown in 50% lunar regolith. 
The mean plant quality averaged across the entire experiment period indicated 
that the controls were of the highest quality. For both the pea and wheat 
treatments, and the wheat treatments, quality was lowest for the two higher 
concentrations of lunar regolith. The plant quality for the lower concentrations 
of lunar regolith tended to be higher. 
Overall wheat height tended to increase until approximately day 
20 of the experiment at which point plant height tended to 
plateau. It did appear that during the last measurement, wheat in 
the controls continued to gain height, whereas wheat associated 
with lunar regolith appears to have decreased in most cases.

We chose to plant wheat because of its many uses as flour in baked goods, pasta, noodles, and lots of other foods, 
which will provide the astronauts with a food source that with is rich in antioxidants, vitamins, minerals, and 
fiber, and that it is fairly easy to grow wheat probably won’t hurt.1 The spring peas provide food for our astronauts, 
and they produce flowers for a short period of time which has some mental benefits for the space travelers like 
improving moods, increasing their level of compassion, boosting their memory especially through smell, and 
reducing stress, which will help them cope better with the challenges they face in their new environment. Besides 
tasting delicious the spring peas are a good source of vitamin C and E, Zinc and other antioxidants that supports 
our immune system which will help keep our astronauts fed and healthy.2 We chose to test the wheat and peas in 
different ratios of Lunar regolith and compost as to minimize the amount of materials needed to be transported 
from Earth the Moon and thereby saving space on the shuttle and money. 
The conclusion 
The Cub Scouts’ hypothesis that the wheat would grow taller in the pots with peas did not seem to be supported 
by our date collected of the wheat’s height in the different pots with different lunar regolith and compost ratios. 
So it does not appear that there is a symbiotic relationship between wheat and peas. At the end of our growth 
period all pots with only wheat were taller than the wheat/pea combos with the exception of the 600g of Lunar 
regolith and 400g compost in pot #2 and #6. When looking at the biomass in the pots with wheat and peas it 
unlike the Cub Scouts prediction seems like the biomass increased when going from 50% to 70% of Lunar 
regolith, however the highest ratio of Lunar regolith with 75% seemed to lower the biomass, indicating that 70% 
of Lunar regolith will be the sweet spot. For the wheat only pots the 60% Lunar regolith produced the most 
biomass. Interestingly most of the pots that contained lunar regolith resulted in a growth plateau around day 20, 
then followed by a decrease in height, but for the peas the height seemed to be less influenced by the Lunar 
regolith content. If we were to improve on our experiment for future testing, it would be interesting to see if wheat
